name: Substantive Testing at Full Coverage
title: Substantive Testing at Full Coverage
answer: Substantive testing at full coverage means testing every transaction or balance in a population rather than sampling a subset of it. In continuous audit and assurance, this shifts the auditor's question from how large a sample is needed to whether the whole population can be tested directly. The scope covers journal entries, ledger balances, reconciliations and transaction streams that feed a financial statement assertion. It applies wherever a population is held in a system that can be queried in full, which in practice means most digital accounting data.

sections.body: Substantive testing at full coverage means testing every transaction or balance in a population rather than sampling a subset of it. In continuous audit and assurance, this shifts the auditor's question from how large a sample is needed to whether the whole population can be tested directly. The scope covers journal entries, ledger balances, reconciliations and transaction streams that feed a financial statement assertion. It applies wherever a population is held in a system that can be queried in full, which in practice means most digital accounting data.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Full coverage testing runs on the client's accounting and ERP systems, on audit data extraction tools, and increasingly on cloud platforms that hold the general ledger and subledgers. Analysts query the full population through SQL, scripting or audit specific analytics software, and results are staged into a working paper environment. The infrastructure requirement is reliable, repeatable access to the source data, not raw compute power. Where data sits across several systems, a mapping and reconciliation layer is needed before any test can run.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with defining the assertion and the population, then extracting the complete set of records for the period. Tests are written as rules or models that flag exceptions, such as duplicate payments, entries posted outside normal hours, or balances that fail a reconciliation check. Every flagged item is investigated, and the auditor records both the rule applied and the disposition of each exception. Because the whole population is tested, the evidence is a complete exception list rather than a statistical inference from a sample.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Full coverage testing changes the evidence trail, so the audit file must show how the population was defined, when it was extracted, and whether it changed after extraction. Access controls, data retention and privacy rules apply to the extracted data just as they do to the source system. Where tests rely on automated rules or models, the auditor needs to document how those rules were built, tested and version controlled. Professional standards on audit evidence and documentation still govern the work, and the auditor remains responsible for the conclusion regardless of how the testing was performed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Coverage is moving from periodic full population tests toward continuous monitoring, where rules run against the ledger as transactions post. That raises new questions about how much testing is enough when everything is tested, and how to avoid alert fatigue from large exception volumes. Audit teams are also working out how to combine full coverage testing with the sampling still required for physical inventory, confirmations and estimates. The direction is toward testing the whole population by default, with human judgement concentrated on the exceptions and on the design of the tests themselves.
